title: Shami v. Commissioner
articleTitle: Judicial Standards of Substantiation and the Evolution of the Research and Development Tax Credit: An Exhaustive Analysis of Shami v. Commissioner and its Regulatory Legacy
subject: Qualified Research Expenses / Documentation
summary: Shami v. Commissioner is a leading federal R&D tax credit case in which the U.S. Tax Court (T.C. Memo. 2012-78) and the Fifth Circuit (741 F.3d 560, 2014) disallowed multi-million-dollar executive wage QREs claimed by Farouk Systems' S corporation shareholders under IRC Section 41, holding that uncorroborated time estimates and second-tier supervision cannot substantiate the credit.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

The litigation in Shami v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue—spanning the United States Tax Court’s trial decision in T.C. Memo. 2012-78 (filed March 21, 2012) and the subsequent appellate ruling by the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit in 741 F.3d 560 (decided January 23, 2014)—stands as one of the most consequential judicial precedents governing the substantiation of the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under Section 41 of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC). The decisions address a recurring point of friction in federal tax controversy: the aggressive inclusion of multi-million-dollar executive compensation packages within Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) based on retrospective, uncorroborated time estimates rather than contemporaneous documentary proof.
Corporate Profile and the Taxpayer's Claim

The underlying corporate taxpayer generating the claimed tax credits was Farouk Systems, Inc. (FSI), a Texas-based enterprise founded by hairdresser and entrepreneur Farouk Shami. FSI develops, manufactures, and distributes commercial hair care, skin, and nail cosmetic products, achieving global prominence through its CHI and BioSilk product lines. During the tax years at issue—2003, 2004, and 2005—FSI elected to be taxed as a Subchapter S corporation pursuant to IRC §§ 1361(a)(1) and 1363(a). Because an S corporation is a pass-through entity taxed in the same manner as an individual, FSI did not pay federal income taxes at the corporate level; instead, its income, deductions, losses, and Section 41 research credits flowed through pro rata to its individual shareholders, who were the consolidated Petitioners before the court (Basim Shami, Rania Ardah, Arthur J. Goertz, Jo McCall Goertz, Farouk Shami, Izziah Shami, Shaukat Gulamani, Rami Shami, Najat Badran, John McCall, and Kathy McCall).

Throughout the 2003 through 2005 period, FSI employed several hundred personnel organized into departments including manufacturing, marketing, sales, education, and research and development. Scientific research, chemical formulation, and laboratory experimentation were either outsourced or conducted within FSI's R&D department, which employed between 18 and 27 staff members—including chemists, technicians, and a vice president of research and development who supervised the department—during the relevant years.

To evaluate its eligibility for federal research credits, FSI engaged alliantgroup, LP, a specialty tax consulting firm, to conduct retrospective R&D tax credit studies covering the 2003, 2004, and 2005 tax years. Relying on the conclusions of these studies, FSI claimed total QREs—comprising in-house wages and supplies (the studies identified wage QREs of $16,325,517, $11,530,159, and $4,016,456 and supply QREs of $431,489, $0, and $3,769 for 2003, 2004, and 2005, respectively)—that generated net Section 41 tax credits of $1,072,170 in 2003, $749,460 in 2004, and $261,315 in 2005. In 2003 alone, FSI ultimately claimed $16,063,430 in total wage QREs on its federal tax filings.

The structural centerpiece of the alliantgroup studies was the allocation of executive compensation to qualified research. Although FSI maintained an active laboratory staff of up to 27 personnel, over 80 percent of the total wage QREs claimed by FSI in each of the three tax years stemmed from the compensation paid to just two senior corporate executives: Farouk Shami and John McCall. Farouk Shami served as Chairman of FSI's Board of Directors throughout 2003, 2004, and 2005, and additionally served as FSI's President and Chief Executive Officer in 2003 (the Tax Court's findings of fact further describe him as FSI's chief executive officer, president, and secretary for 2003 and 2004). FSI paid Shami annual wages ranging between approximately $8.0 million and $9.5 million during the credit years ($8,735,727 for 2003, $7,988,310 for 2004, and $9,529,639 for 2005). Petitioners claimed that Shami devoted 80 percent of his working time in 2003 and 2004, and 35 percent of his time in 2005, to qualified research services. By claiming time allocations right at the 80 percent regulatory threshold in 2003 and 2004, FSI invoked the "substantially all" rule of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d)(2) to sweep 100 percent of Shami's multi-million-dollar wage compensation into its QRE calculation.

Similarly, John McCall served as Co-Chairman of FSI's Board of Directors and Executive Vice President in 2003 and 2004, while also acting as a principal in a separate company that distributed FSI products. FSI paid McCall annual wages of $5,722,699 in 2003 and $1,839,581 in 2004. Petitioners claimed that McCall likewise spent 80 percent of his time in 2003 and 2004 performing qualified research services, thereby including 100 percent of his compensation as QREs for those two years. Neither Farouk Shami nor John McCall possessed any formal education or training in chemistry, engineering, or any other physical or biological science.

body.text: The Tax Authority's Challenge and Trial Narrowing

Following a comprehensive examination, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue issued statutory Notices of Deficiency to the FSI shareholders, disallowing the claimed Section 41 research credits in their entirety and assessing corresponding federal income tax deficiencies. The shareholders filed timely petitions for redetermination with the U.S. Tax Court under Docket Nos. 28666-08, 28667-08, 28673-08, and related consolidated dockets.

During the four-day bench trial before Judge Diane L. Kroupa, the scope of the controversy narrowed substantially through concessions by both parties. On the second day of trial, counsel for the IRS stated in open court that the government could see that "experimentation [was] taking place" and agreed not to dispute the wage QREs claimed by FSI for employees other than four highly compensated employees. The Commissioner thus narrowed its challenge to the wage QREs claimed for four highly compensated FSI employees: Farouk Shami, John McCall, and two other highly compensated employees. Petitioners later conceded that the wages paid to the other two highly compensated employees did not constitute legitimate QREs.

Consequently, the sole substantive factual dispute tried before the Tax Court was whether, and to what extent, the wages paid to Shami (for 2003, 2004, and 2005) and McCall (for 2003 and 2004) qualified as in-house research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(2). However, during post-trial deficiency computations under Tax Court Rule 155, a secondary procedural dispute emerged when the Commissioner’s final deficiency calculation continued to disallow supply-cost QREs claimed by FSI for the 2003 and 2005 tax years.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The dispute in Shami was adjudicated exclusively under the federal internal revenue laws of the United States, centering on the interplay between IRC § 41, IRC § 174, IRC § 6001, and their corresponding Treasury Regulations. Under IRC § 41(a)(1) and § 41(c), a taxpayer is allowed a credit against federal income tax equal to 20 percent of the excess (if any) of the taxpayer's total QREs for the credit year over a statutory base amount. The base amount is computed as the product of the taxpayer's fixed-base percentage and average annual gross receipts for the four preceding taxable years, subject to a statutory floor under which the base amount cannot be less than 50 percent of current-year QREs.

Under IRC § 41(b)(1) and (2), QREs encompass in-house research expenses, which consist of any "wages" (defined by reference to IRC § 3401(a) income tax withholding wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)) paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services" performed by such employee, alongside any amount paid or incurred for "supplies" used in the conduct of qualified research. IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c) strictly limit "qualified services" to employees who are either engaging directly in qualified research, or engaging in the "direct supervision or direct support" of research activities that constitute qualified research. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(2), qualifying "direct supervision" means the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research, such as a laboratory scientist who directly supervises bench experiments. The regulation expressly excludes supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that upper-level executive is personally a qualified research scientist.

When an employee performs both qualified and nonqualified services during a taxable year, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d)(1) mandates that only the amount of wages allocated to the performance of qualified services constitutes an in-house research expense. Absent a demonstrably more appropriate alternative method, this allocation is computed by multiplying the employee's total annual wages by a ratio whose numerator is the total hours spent performing qualified services during the year and whose denominator is the total hours worked by the employee across all services during the year. However, under the "substantially all" safe harbor of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d)(2), if at least 80 percent of the employee's wages/time during the taxable year are attributable to qualified services, 100 percent of the employee's annual wages qualify as QREs.

For underlying activities to constitute "qualified research," the taxpayer must satisfy the cumulative Four-Part Test of IRC § 41(d)(1) separately for each business component. First, under the Section 174 Test (§ 41(d)(1)(A)), the expenditures must qualify as research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174—meaning they are incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business, represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design of a product or process, and are "reasonable under the circumstances" pursuant to IRC § 174(e). Second, under the Technological Information Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(i)), the activity must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, relying on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the Business Component Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3)), the application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component (any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business) for a qualified purpose—specifically a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality—whereas research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors is expressly disqualified under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B). Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test (§ 41(d)(1)(C)), substantially all (defined by regulation as 80 percent or more, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis) of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation involving the systematic evaluation of alternatives to resolve technical uncertainty.

Finally, the procedural posture of any R&D credit dispute is governed by IRC § 6001, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d), and Tax Court Rule 142(a). Because Congress enacted stricter eligibility requirements in 1986 out of concern that taxpayers were claiming the credit for virtually any product development expense, and because tax credits are a matter of legislative grace, the Commissioner’s deficiency determinations are presumed correct and the taxpayer bears the burden of proving entitlement to the credit (Welch v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111, 115 (1933)); in Shami, that burden remained with Petitioners because they did not show compliance with the burden-shifting requirements of IRC § 7491(a). Under IRC § 6001 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d) (as amended by T.D. 9104 in 2004), a taxpayer claiming a Section 41 credit must retain records in "sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit".
The Courts' Final Holdings

In T.C. Memo. 2012-78, the U.S. Tax Court ruled entirely in favor of the Commissioner. Judge Kroupa held that Petitioners failed to provide any documentation establishing how much time, if any, Farouk Shami or John McCall spent performing qualified research services during 2003, 2004, or 2005, and that the testimony offered was inadequate to substantiate that time. The Tax Court found the testimony of the two FSI employees general, vague, and conclusory, noted that several witnesses contradicted Shami's testimony and that no witness corroborated McCall's, and found all of Petitioners' testimony self-serving and unreliable. Furthermore, the Tax Court refused to estimate a reduced QRE allocation under the Cohan doctrine (Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930)), holding that the complete absence of credible evidence left the court with no reasonable basis upon which to formulate an estimate. In entering final decisions, the Tax Court also concluded that the Commissioner had not conceded the supply-cost issue and adopted the Commissioner's deficiency computations, which disallowed FSI's claimed supply QREs for 2003 and 2005.

On appeal in 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed in part, vacated in part, and remanded. First, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the Tax Court's evidentiary ruling under Federal Rule of Evidence 403, holding that the trial judge did not abuse her discretion by refusing to admit over 4,500 pages of raw laboratory test records and limiting Petitioners to sample records, as the excluded documents were cumulative and lacked probative value regarding executive time allocations. Second, the appellate court affirmed the complete disallowance of Shami's and McCall's wage QREs, holding that the Tax Court applied the proper statutory burden of proof; that Petitioners waived their Cohan estimation argument through inadequate briefing and, alternatively, that Williams v. United States, 245 F.2d 559 (5th Cir. 1957) foreclosed mandatory estimation where the record lacks a reliable evidentiary foundation; that the Tax Court did not clearly err in implicitly concluding that Petitioners had not proven Shami engaged in "direct supervision" under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(2), because the stipulations suggested that Shami was an upper-level manager to whom FSI's Vice President of R&D reported—rather than a "first-line" direct supervisor—and said nothing about the time, if any, Shami spent directly supervising qualified research; and that Shami's status as a named inventor on a patent did not substantiate Section 41 wage allocations (an argument also held waived). Third, the Fifth Circuit vacated the Tax Court's deficiency judgments regarding the 2003 and 2005 supply costs and remanded the cases, holding—while assuming without deciding that an oral, on-record concession is equivalent to a stipulation under Tax Court Rule 91—that the plain meaning of IRS trial counsel's on-the-record statements narrowing the dispute to the QREs of highly compensated employees constituted a binding concession, and that the Tax Court abused its discretion by implicitly relieving the Commissioner of that concession without evaluating whether "justice requires" such relief.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of over 80 percent of FSI’s claimed wage QREs resulted from a compounding series of legal, technical, and evidentiary failures. An examination of the trial and appellate opinions reveals six distinct structural vulnerabilities that doomed the taxpayer's executive compensation claim while exposing a critical procedural error by the government on supply costs.
Unsubstantiated Executive Time Allocations and Abuse of the 80 Percent Substantially All Rule

The foundational failure in Shami was the complete absence of contemporaneous or verifiable documentation establishing a factual nexus between the multi-million-dollar salaries paid to Shami and McCall and the performance of qualified services. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d)(1), when an employee performs both qualified research services and general executive, administrative, or commercial duties, the taxpayer must apportion wages via the time ratio:
Qualified Wages = Total Annual Wages × (Time Spent Performing Qualified Services ÷ Total Time Spent Performing All Services)

However, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d)(2) provides a powerful administrative cliff: if that fraction equals or exceeds 80 percent (qualified time ÷ total time ≥ 0.80), 100 percent of the employee's annual wages are treated as QREs. In the litigation, Petitioners claimed that both Shami and McCall spent 80 percent of their time performing qualified services in 2003 and 2004 (and that Shami spent 35 percent in 2005). Because Shami served as Chairman and (at least in 2003) President and CEO of a company employing several hundred workers—and McCall served as Co-Chairman and Executive Vice President of FSI while also being a principal of a separate product distribution entity—claiming that both executives spent four out of every five working hours performing hands-on laboratory research or first-line bench supervision strained facial credibility.

When challenged by the IRS, Petitioners could not produce a single timesheet, calendar, appointment book, project log, electronic laboratory notebook entry, or contemporaneous memorandum recording the hours either executive spent on R&D versus corporate governance, marketing, sales, or distribution. While Judge Kroupa acknowledged that Petitioners were not required to prove that "Mr. Shami and Mr. McCall wore lab coats," the court emphasized that where product research and development is dispersed across numerous corporate departments and conducted by many employees, the taxpayer must provide objective evidence quantifying the time spent by executives on qualified services versus all other nonqualified services.

Furthermore, the Fifth Circuit cited the statutory constraint of IRC § 174(e), which dictates that an expenditure qualifies under Section 174 (and by extension Section 41(d)(1)(A)) only to the extent that the amount thereof is "reasonable under the circumstances," and faulted Petitioners for making no attempt to explain how much of Shami's wages could be attributed to his patented invention or that such amount was reasonable. Although neither court ruled on whether the executives' compensation levels were themselves unreasonable, allocating up to approximately $9.5 million per year of a single executive's wages—an executive with no formal scientific or engineering training—to qualified research required credible evidence of the time actually spent on qualified services, which the record did not contain.
The Direct Supervision Fallacy and Multi-Tiered Organizational Hierarchies

Recognizing that neither Shami nor McCall possessed formal training in chemistry or engineering to conduct bench-level chemical formulation independently, Petitioners argued on appeal that Shami's wages qualified under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) because he engaged in the "direct supervision" of qualified research. Petitioners contended that the Tax Court failed to consider direct supervision and ignored the evidence, asserting that because the Commissioner conceded the QREs of FSI employees whom Shami supervised, Shami by definition performed qualified services.

The Fifth Circuit dismantled this argument by strictly enforcing the hierarchical boundary codified in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(2). Under that regulation, qualifying "direct supervision" is restricted exclusively to the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research, illustrated in the regulatory text by a research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments. Conversely, the regulation explicitly excludes supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that higher-level manager is personally a qualified research scientist. The Fifth Circuit distilled this regulatory mandate into an unmistakable bright-line judicial rule: "In short, the supervisor of the direct supervisor of employees who conduct qualified research is not himself engaged in qualified research".

The Fifth Circuit further held that the record did not establish that Shami was a first-line direct supervisor, finding that the only stipulation addressing his supervisory role was inconclusive. The parties had stipulated on the record that beginning April 26, 2004, and continuing throughout 2005, Ali Ghannad served as Vice President of R&D for FSI, that his duties included developing new products, managing the laboratory, managing quality control, and managing quality assurance, and that Ali Ghannad reported to Shami. The appellate court analyzed the two-fold legal impact of this stipulation. While Ghannad's involvement in "developing new products" offered some support for the contention that Shami engaged in some direct supervision of some qualified research, the stipulation also provided that Ghannad was FSI's R&D manager and therefore suggested that Shami was an upper-level manager who supervised the FSI employees who, in turn, supervised the performance of qualified research. Two other stipulations stated that FSI's laboratory technicians reported to FSI employees other than Shami. Consequently, with respect to the 18 to 27 chemists and technicians conducting experimentation in the laboratory, the record pointed to supervisors other than Shami as their direct supervisors (the opinion does not identify James Sie's role at FSI beyond describing him as a former FSI employee who testified for the Commissioner). The court also held that the Commissioner's trial concession could not bear the weight Petitioners placed on it, because it was general, could encompass QREs based on direct supervision, and was entirely consistent with Shami—as the head supervisor at FSI—not performing qualified services. Because second-tier supervision falls outside IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), and because the stipulations and concessions said nothing about the time (if any) Shami spent directly supervising FSI employees engaged in qualified research, the Fifth Circuit held that the Tax Court's implicit conclusion that Petitioners had not proven direct supervision was not clearly erroneous.
Evidentiary Deficiencies, Non-Probative Laboratory Records, and Witness Credibility Collapse

Petitioners attempted to bridge their documentation gap through two evidentiary mechanisms at trial: proffering over 4,500 pages of internal laboratory test records and presenting oral testimony from four witnesses. Both strategies collapsed under scrutiny.
Exclusion of Bulk Laboratory Records Under FRE 403

At trial, Judge Kroupa refused to admit the entirety of Petitioners' 4,500+ pages of raw laboratory testing records, limiting Petitioners instead to dozens of sample records (comprising several hundred pages). On appeal, Petitioners argued that excluding the bulk records constituted an abuse of discretion, and further asserted that they had used samples only because the Commissioner's counsel had conceded, during an unrecorded pretrial telephone status conference, that the Commissioner would not challenge the sufficiency of available documentary substantiation. The Fifth Circuit also rejected the alleged pretrial concession as absent from the record and in conflict with the Commissioner's position reflected in the record, including counsel's statement at a May 24, 2010 discovery hearing that the case presented "a substantiation question".

Applying Federal Rule of Evidence 403—which applies to U.S. Tax Court proceedings via IRC § 7453 and authorizes a trial judge to exclude relevant evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by considerations of undue delay, waste of time, or needlessly presenting cumulative evidence—the Fifth Circuit affirmed the exclusion. A review of the admitted sample records revealed why the remaining 4,500 pages had only minimal probative value. Not a single sample laboratory record mentioned John McCall or indicated that he performed any service whatsoever. Only a few dozen of the several hundred pages submitted reflected that Farouk Shami "approved" the document. Crucially, the Fifth Circuit found it unclear what "approving" a document meant and noted that Petitioners did not elaborate in their briefing, so the records did not show whether Shami was validating a scientific formulation hypothesis or merely exercising commercial, marketing, or aesthetic sign-off (the opinion did not itself address IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)'s style, taste, and cosmetic exclusion). Moreover, the documentary evidence was silent about the amount of time Shami spent reviewing or approving any test. Because Petitioners themselves had described the admitted records as examples meant to educate the court without introducing all of the records, and because those samples were devoid of evidence of Shami's and McCall's performance of qualified services, the Fifth Circuit held that introducing further records would plainly have been a waste of time under FRE 403.
Collapse of Uncorroborated and Contradicted Oral Testimony

Because the documentary evidence—including internal memoranda and e-mails reporting product-test results to Shami, with no responsive memoranda or e-mails from Shami—said little about whether Shami performed qualified services and nothing about McCall, Petitioners' case rested primarily on the oral testimony of Farouk Shami, John McCall, FSI Creative Director Jason Yates, and FSI Chemist Tai Pham. Judge Kroupa found the testimony of the two FSI employees general, vague, and conclusory and found all of Petitioners' testimony self-serving and unreliable; the Fifth Circuit, in affirming, described the testimony as "contradictory, self-serving, and noncredible".

The credibility collapse was driven in part by contrary testimony from former FSI employees. The Commissioner called James Sie and Ali Ghannad—former FSI employees, with Ghannad having served as FSI's Vice President of R&D from April 26, 2004 through 2005—whose testimony contradicted the testimony offered by Petitioners, although the opinion does not detail the specific points of contradiction. Meanwhile, no witness corroborated McCall's testimony at all. The Fifth Circuit highlighted that all of Petitioners' witnesses had an incentive to mislead: as the principal shareholders in FSI, Shami and McCall would be hurt if the deficiency were upheld, and Yates and Pham were both FSI employees at the time of trial. Following settled appellate doctrine, the Fifth Circuit held that a trial judge's credibility assessments will not be disturbed except in the "very rarest of circumstances," affirming the total disregard of Petitioners' testimonial case.
Misapplication of the Cohan Estimation Doctrine and Intra-Circuit Precedent Resolution

Faced with the collapse of their 80 percent allocation claim, Petitioners invoked the judicial estimation doctrine of Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), as applied to Section 41 R&D credits by the Fifth Circuit in United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009). Under Cohan, if a taxpayer proves that they paid or incurred a deductible expense or qualified credit expenditure but cannot substantiate the exact dollar amount, the court should make "as close an approximation as it can, bearing heavily if it chooses upon the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of his own making". Before the Tax Court, Petitioners argued that the court must estimate the amount of wages allocable to qualified services if it found that either Shami or McCall performed qualified services; on appeal, they asserted that FSI's use of estimates of the executives' time was "indisputably permissible," citing McFerrin. Connected to this argument was Petitioners' claim, citing the legislative history of § 41, that the Tax Court imposed an inappropriately high "standard of exactitude" by requiring specific documentary evidence, including time records, of the allocation between qualifying and non-qualifying costs—whereas, as the Fifth Circuit noted, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d) and the accompanying Treasury guidance (including T.D. 9104) do not require records to be kept in a particular manner beyond the requirements of IRC § 6001.

The Fifth Circuit rejected this argument on both procedural and substantive grounds, establishing a critical doctrinal precedent for tax litigation in the process. Procedurally, in their opening brief, Petitioners devoted only a single conclusory sentence and a bare citation to McFerrin to support their estimation claim. Under Fifth Circuit precedent (citing Coury v. Moss, 529 F.3d 579, 587 (5th Cir. 2008)), failure to brief an issue adequately constitutes waiver. Furthermore, the Fifth Circuit clarified that the Tax Court did not demand timesheets or any specific category of document; rather, it simply required some credible evidence (documentary or testimonial) proving that the executives performed qualified services.

Addressing the merits in the alternative, the Fifth Circuit resolved a perceived tension within its own circuit precedent regarding the Cohan rule. While McFerrin (decided in 2009) stated that a court "should" estimate QREs if qualified activities are proved, the Fifth Circuit pointed to its much earlier decision in Williams v. United States, 245 F.2d 559, 560 (5th Cir. 1957). In Williams, the Fifth Circuit held that while a trial court possesses discretion to make an estimate under Cohan, it may not be compelled to do so—even where an estimate, if made, might have been affirmed—because the basic requirement is sufficient evidence in the record to satisfy the trier of fact that at least the estimated amount was actually spent or incurred for the stated purpose; until the trier has that assurance, relief to the taxpayer would be "unguided largesse". The court explained that Cohan is not implicated unless the taxpayer first proves entitlement to some tax benefit (i.e., proving that Shami and McCall personally performed some qualified services), a finding the Tax Court never made; it further declined to read McFerrin as holding that Cohan is untempered by exceptions and, invoking the principle that when panel opinions appear to conflict the earlier opinion controls (the Fifth Circuit's "rule of orderliness"), held that even assuming a conflict, Williams governs. Moreover, once the Tax Court properly discredited Petitioners' self-serving testimony, the evidentiary record contained zero reliable foundation upon which to base an estimate, rendering the refusal to apply Cohan entirely proper under Williams.
Overreliance on the Patent Safe Harbor Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii)

Petitioners also asserted that because Farouk Shami was credited as an inventor on several patents, those patents conclusively proved that he was involved in, and in control of every element of, the research conducted at FSI—although the Fifth Circuit noted that only one patent, on which Shami is listed as a coinventor, appeared to relate to research conducted during the tax years at issue.

Aside from holding the argument waived for inadequate briefing in the opening brief, the Fifth Circuit exposed the fundamental legal flaw in conflating patent ownership with Section 41 wage QRE substantiation. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii)—commonly known as the "Patent Safe Harbor"—the issuance of a patent (other than a design patent under 35 U.S.C. § 171) is conclusive evidence only that the taxpayer has discovered information that is technological in nature and intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component (satisfying IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and part of the § 174 uncertainty test). However, the Patent Safe Harbor does not establish that the underlying costs were reasonable under IRC § 174(e), nor that substantially all of the activities constituted a process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C). Most importantly, the Fifth Circuit explained that the taxpayer must tie the research underlying the patent to the specific business component affected by the patent—so that a patent on a discrete business component does not mean all of the taxpayer's research is qualified—and faulted Petitioners for making no attempt to explain how much of Shami's wages could be attributed to the patented invention, whether that amount was reasonable, how Shami's alleged activities constituted a process of experimentation, or how the patent related to the variety of FSI products he allegedly developed during 2003 through 2005; the patent therefore did not establish the quantum of wages allocable to qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d).
Procedural Litigation Dynamics: Tax Court Rule 91 and the Supply QRE Reversal

The sole bright spot for the taxpayer in Shami occurred on appeal regarding FSI's claimed supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) for tax years 2003 and 2005. In the Notices of Deficiency, the IRS had disallowed the entire research credit, which implicitly encompassed both wage QREs and supply QREs. However, during the four-day trial, counsel for the Commissioner repeatedly made explicit statements on the record narrowing the scope of the government's case, acknowledging that "experimentation is taking place," agreeing to "focus in on" the highly compensated employees, and—when clarifying what the Commissioner perceived to be the remaining issues in the case—identifying only the QREs related to Shami and McCall; counsel also agreed with Petitioners' counsel's statement that "the only question" remaining was the QREs related to Shami and McCall, and the Commissioner's post-trial brief stated that only those QREs were at issue.

Consistent with these open-court representations, Petitioners presented no documentary or testimonial evidence regarding supply costs during the trial. Yet, following the opinion in T.C. Memo. 2012-78, the Commissioner submitted deficiency calculations that disallowed the 2003 and 2005 supply QREs, and the Tax Court—concluding that the Commissioner had not conceded the supply-cost issue—entered judgment adopting the government's figures.

The Fifth Circuit vacated this portion of the judgment, grounding its analysis in Tax Court Rule 91. Rule 91 does not refer to oral stipulations or concessions at trial; both parties assumed that an oral concession is binding, consistent with existing Tax Court precedent (e.g., Church of Scientology of Cal. v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 381 (1984)), and the Fifth Circuit assumed without deciding that an oral, on-record concession is equivalent to a stipulation. Under Rule 91(e), a stipulation is binding upon the parties according to its plain meaning—even where it creates a windfall for the taxpayer—and a court will not permit a party to qualify, change, or contradict a stipulation in whole or in part except where "justice requires". The Fifth Circuit held that, although the Commissioner may have intended the concession to encompass only wage QREs, the plain meaning of the IRS counsel's trial statements, viewed together and in context, was a concession that the IRS would not challenge FSI's claimed QREs—including supply costs—except those related to the wages of the highly compensated employees. By adopting the Commissioner's post-trial deficiency numbers without evaluating whether "justice required" releasing the IRS from its on-the-record concession, the Tax Court abused its discretion, necessitating vacatur and remand for a recalculation of the shareholders' deficiencies.

Relied on retrospective consulting studies by alliantgroup without retaining contemporaneous records, calendars, or project logs linking executive activities to qualified research.

While T.D. 9104 provides reasonable flexibility and does not mandate a specific document type, the taxpayer must still establish a credible evidentiary nexus between claimed expenditures and qualified services. Disallowance Affirmed.
Executive Wage Apportionment & The 80% "Substantially All" Rule

Wages must be apportioned via the ratio of qualified service hours to total hours worked; if ≥ 80% of wages are attributable to qualified services, 100% of wages qualify. Amounts must be reasonable under the circumstances (§ 174(e)).

Claimed 80% time allocations in 2003–2004 (and 35% for Shami in 2005) for two top executives without formal scientific or engineering training earning approximately $1.8M–$9.5M annually, whose wages accounted for over 80% of FSI's total wage QREs, with no documentation establishing the time spent.

Where product development spans multiple departments and executives hold vast commercial/administrative duties, uncorroborated percentage claims fail to substantiate either the 80% cliff or fractional allocation. Disallowance Affirmed.
Direct Supervision of Qualified Research
Qualifying "direct supervision" is strictly limited to immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research; higher-level managers to whom first-line managers report are excluded.

Stipulated that VP of R&D Ali Ghannad (April 26, 2004 through 2005) developed new products, managed the lab, quality control, and quality assurance, and reported to Shami, while other stipulations showed laboratory technicians reported to employees other than Shami—suggesting Shami was an upper-level (second-tier) manager.

"The supervisor of the direct supervisor of employees who conduct qualified research is not himself engaged in qualified research." Even if the stipulation offered some support for some direct supervision, nothing in the record addressed the time Shami spent on any direct supervision; the Tax Court's implicit finding was not clearly erroneous. Disallowance Affirmed.
Admissibility of Bulk Technical Records
IRC § 7453; Federal Rule of Evidence (FRE) 403
Relevant evidence may be excluded if its probative value is substantially outweighed by undue delay, waste of time, or needless presentation of cumulative evidence.

Attempted to admit over 4,500 pages of raw laboratory test records; the admitted samples did not mention McCall, and only a few dozen of several hundred pages showed that Shami "approved" a document, without explaining what "approval" meant or the time spent.

Trial courts have broad discretion under FRE 403 to limit parties to representative samples when bulk records are cumulative and lack probative value on the disputed issue of executive time allocation. Exclusion Affirmed.
Oral Testimony & Witness Credibility
Tax Court Rule 142(a); Fifth Circuit Clear Error Standard of Review
Oral testimony offered to substantiate tax credits must be specific, credible, corroborated, and consistent with objective record facts.

Offered general, vague, conclusory, and self-serving testimony from Shami, McCall, and two then-current FSI employees (Yates and Pham), which was uncorroborated (as to McCall) or contradicted by former FSI employees James Sie and Ali Ghannad.

Trial court need not accept self-serving, uncorroborated, or contradicted testimony; appellate courts will not overturn credibility assessments except in the "very rarest of circumstances". Disallowance Affirmed.
Judicial Estimation Under the Cohan Rule
Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930); United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009); Williams v. United States, 245 F.2d 559 (5th Cir. 1957)
A court may approximate an expense if the taxpayer first proves entitlement to some tax benefit and provides a reasonable evidentiary foundation for the estimate.
Adequately briefed neither Cohan nor McFerrin in the opening appellate brief (waiver), and demanded mandatory estimation despite failing to prove Shami or McCall performed any qualified services.

Even assuming any conflict, Williams (the earlier panel opinion) controls over McFerrin: Cohan estimation is discretionary, cannot be compelled, and is barred where lack of credible evidence would turn an estimate into "unguided largesse". Refusal to Estimate Affirmed.
The Patent Safe Harbor
Issuance of a utility patent is conclusive evidence that the taxpayer discovered technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty regarding a business component.

Made only a bare, unsupported assertion in the opening brief (with slightly more support offered for the first time in the reply brief) that Shami's patents conclusively proved he controlled every element of FSI's research; only one patent naming Shami as coinventor appeared to relate to 2003–2005 research.

Patent issuance satisfies only part of the qualified research test; the taxpayer must still prove § 174 reasonableness, a process of experimentation, the tie to a specific business component, and the wages allocable to the patented research. Argument Waived; Alternatively Rejected.
Binding Effect of Trial Concessions on Supply QREs
IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii); Tax Court Rule 91; Rule 155

Assuming without deciding that on-the-record oral concessions by counsel operate as stipulations under Rule 91, they must be enforced according to their plain meaning unless "justice requires" relief.

IRS counsel stated at trial that the only remaining issues were the QREs related to Shami and McCall, and Petitioners presented no supply evidence, but the IRS later disallowed 2003 and 2005 supply QREs in post-trial computations.

The Tax Court abused its discretion by implicitly relieving the Commissioner of the plain meaning of its open-court concession without evaluating whether justice required relief. Vacated and Remanded in Taxpayer's Favor.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial holdings of Shami v. Commissioner into actionable tax and operational compliance, the following two applied case studies model realistic middle-market enterprises confronting the exact legal, structural, and evidentiary pitfalls identified by the Tax Court and the Fifth Circuit. Each case study details a step-by-step remediation protocol across project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Specialty Chemical and Cosmeceutical Formulation Manufacturer
Industry Context and Initial Vulnerability Profile

Luminary BioCosmetics, Inc. (LBC) is a closely held Subchapter S corporation based in Houston, Texas, generating $85 million in annual gross receipts through the development and manufacture of professional salon hair-bonding treatments, thermal protectant polymers, and UV-cured nail elastomers. The company employs 180 personnel, including an internal R&D laboratory staffed by 14 formulation chemists, 4 stability technicians, and a PhD Vice President of Research & Formulation, Dr. Elena Rostova. During the current tax year, LBC undertook Project Keratin-Shield, an initiative to formulate a novel, ammonia-free, thermal-activated disulfide bond-crosslinking serum capable of withstanding high-temperature flat-iron styling without degrading hair tensile strength or releasing volatile siloxanes. LBC's Founder and CEO, Marcus Vance (a former master salon stylist with no formal degree in chemistry), receives $4.2 million in W-2 wages, while LBC's Executive Vice President of Brand Strategy, Sarah Jenkins, receives $1.6 million in W-2 wages.

Prior to legal intervention, LBC's outside tax preparer proposed claiming 80 percent of Vance's and Jenkins's wages as QREs—sweeping 100 percent of their combined $5.8 million compensation into the credit computation via the Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d)(2) "substantially all" rule. The preparer based this position on four fragile premises: first, that Vance and Jenkins conceptually originated Project Keratin-Shield, walked through the laboratory weekly to test product texture and fragrance on hair swatches, and supervised Dr. Rostova, who reported directly to Vance; second, that LBC possessed 3,800 pages of laboratory batch tickets and viscosity test printouts bearing Vance's stamped "Approved" signature at the bottom; third, that Vance was listed as a co-inventor alongside Dr. Rostova on a provisional U.S. patent application covering the serum's siloxane-free emulsion vehicle; and fourth, that LBC could claim $450,000 in raw chemical compounds commingled in a general inventory ledger account alongside outsourced dermal sensitization testing performed by DermaTest Labs under an informal purchase order. Under the holdings of Shami, an IRS challenge to this posture would likely result in the complete disallowance of Vance's and Jenkins's wage QREs, the exclusion in litigation of the bulk of the 3,800 batch sheets under FRE 403, and severe challenges to the commingled supplies and uncontracted third-party testing.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Delayering Supervisory Chains

To eliminate the "supervisor of the direct supervisor" defect that defeated Petitioners' direct-supervision argument for Farouk Shami's wages under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(2), LBC must immediately restructure its R&D governance and segregate commercial or aesthetic oversight from first-line scientific supervision. First, LBC must remove EVP Sarah Jenkins entirely from the QRE computation. Her evaluation of product fragrance, sheen, and salon marketability constitutes non-qualifying commercial oversight and falls squarely within the statutory exclusion for research related to "style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors" under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B). Second, so long as Dr. Rostova manages the laboratory and supervises the 14 chemists while reporting to CEO Marcus Vance, Vance is a second-tier manager whose general supervisory time over the R&D department is legally disqualified under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(2) as applied in Shami. However, because Vance possesses specialized empirical expertise in hair fiber cuticle mechanics and actively leads a dedicated Advanced Cuticle Penetration Tiger Team—consisting of two senior chemists assigned to resolve high-temperature cuticle swelling—LBC must execute a formal, contemporaneous Project Charter establishing that those two chemists report directly and exclusively to Vance for bench-level experimental direction on that specific sub-component, bypassing Dr. Rostova. For all other laboratory projects managed by Dr. Rostova, Dr. Rostova's wages—and not Vance's—are claimed as the qualifying first-line direct supervisor.

Furthermore, to insulate the claim against a reasonableness challenge under IRC § 174(e), LBC must address the magnitude of Vance's $4.2 million W-2 compensation. Because Vance's multi-million-dollar salary reflects his role as founder, chief executive, and primary commercial driver of an $85 million enterprise, claiming even a fractional percentage of $4.2 million for bench supervision invites heightened scrutiny of the kind reflected in Shami, where the Fifth Circuit faulted Petitioners for failing to explain how much of Shami's wages was attributable to the patented research or that such amount was reasonable. LBC's Board of Directors must adopt a formal compensation resolution benchmarking the fair market salary of a Chief Technical Formulation Director (for example, $320,000 per annum) and capping the hourly wage rate applied to Vance's documented first-line supervisory hours at that reasonable technical benchmark, while ensuring that S-corporation shareholder returns beyond reasonable W-2 compensation for services are paid as non-wage shareholder distributions rather than inflated W-2 wages.
Step 2: Implementing Contemporaneous Time-Tracking and Abandoning the Artificial 80 Percent Cliff

To prevent the Tax Court from rejecting LBC's wage allocations as uncorroborated guesswork and refusing estimation under Williams v. United States, LBC must replace retrospective year-end oral estimates with a contemporaneous time-apportionment architecture. LBC must abandon the aggressive claim that Vance spent 80 percent of his time on qualified services under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d)(2) and instead apply strict fractional apportionment under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d)(1). Vance, Dr. Rostova, and all 18 laboratory personnel must log their hours weekly in an electronic time-tracking system mapped to granular activity codes that explicitly separate qualified bench experimentation and first-line supervision from aesthetic evaluation, routine quality control, and corporate administration.

body.text: Because the Tax Court in Shami discredited executive testimony when former employees (James Sie and Ali Ghannad) contradicted it at trial years later, LBC must also institute a mandatory quarterly corroboration protocol. At the close of each calendar quarter, Dr. Rostova and the two Tiger Team chemists must review and digitally co-sign Vance's technical time logs, certifying that the recorded first-line supervisory sessions occurred as described. This contemporaneous, multi-party corroborated record neutralizes the risk of future testimonial impeachment if laboratory personnel subsequently leave the company.
Step 3: Re-Engineering Technical Documentation and Patent Nexus

To ensure LBC's laboratory records possess high probative value rather than being excluded as cumulative waste under Federal Rule of Evidence 403, LBC must overhaul its Electronic Laboratory Notebook (ELN) and batch documentation protocols. In Shami, the sample lab records were held to have minimal probative value—and the remaining 4,500+ pages were excluded as cumulative—because it was unclear what Shami's "approval" meant and the records were silent as to the time he spent. LBC must eliminate generic "Approved by CEO" signature stamps on batch sheets and replace them with a structured Technical Review and Supervisory Action Log embedded within each ELN experiment record. Whenever Vance (for the Tiger Team) or Dr. Rostova (for the main lab) reviews a formulation iteration, the ELN entry must capture four mandatory data points: the date and exact start/end timestamps of the supervisory review; the specific technical uncertainty addressed (such as phase separation of bis-aminopropyl diglycol dimaleate at pH 4.2 under high-temperature thermal stress); the specific scientific directive issued by the supervisor to resolve that uncertainty (such as directing the bench chemist to substitute a cationic guar derivative at 1.2% w/w to stabilize zeta potential); and contemporaneous digital authentication by both the supervisor and the bench chemist.

Simultaneously, LBC must properly scope its reliance on the Patent Safe Harbor of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii). LBC will introduce its provisional and utility patent applications solely to establish that Project Keratin-Shield discovered technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i). Rather than claiming the patent proves Vance's wage QREs, LBC will substantiate the Process of Experimentation (§ 41(d)(1)(C)) through the ELN logs documenting the systematic trial-and-error evaluation of 64 distinct cross-linking monomer ratios, and will substantiate wage QREs exclusively through the corroborated timekeeping logs and ELN timestamps.
Step 4: Contractual Restructuring and General Ledger Segregation for Supplies and Contract Research

To protect its non-wage QREs and avoid the post-trial Rule 155 vulnerability that nearly cost FSI its supply credits in Shami, LBC must execute strict accounting and contractual reforms. First, to substantiate supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), LBC must establish a dedicated Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) General Ledger sub-account (GL Account 5120-RD: Laboratory Experimental Consumables) completely segregated from commercial manufacturing raw materials. Every chemical reagent requisitioned for Project Keratin-Shield bench trials or pilot batch destruction testing must be billed to GL 5120-RD using a purchase requisition tied to Project Code R-101. Second, to claim 65 percent of the payments made to DermaTest Labs as contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e), LBC must replace its informal purchase orders with a formal Master Research Services Agreement executed prior to the performance of any testing. That agreement must explicitly stipulate that the testing services are performed on behalf of LBC, that LBC retains exclusive ownership and substantial rights to all resulting data, formulations, and intellectual property without paying additional royalties, and that LBC bears the full financial risk of technical failure, remaining obligated to pay for the research services on an at-risk basis.
Case Study 2: Industrial Manufacturing and Embedded Process Engineering Enterprise
Industry Context and Initial Vulnerability Profile

Apex Composite Autoclaves, Inc. (ACA) is an S corporation headquartered in Baton Rouge, Louisiana—within the appellate jurisdiction of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit—generating $120 million in annual revenue by designing and manufacturing industrial pressure vessels and composite curing systems. ACA employs 250 personnel, including 22 mechanical, thermal, and control-systems engineers led by a Chief Engineer, Robert Miller. During the credit year, ACA launched Project AeroCure-X, an initiative to develop both a next-generation carbon-fiber curing autoclave product (Product Component) and an automated, friction-stir robotic welding assembly line to manufacture the autoclave's pressure hull in-house (Process Component). ACA's Co-Chairman and Executive Vice President of Operations, Thomas Sterling (an MBA with no engineering degree, earning $3.1 million in W-2 compensation), and Vice President of Corporate Development, David Vance (earning $1.4 million), claimed 75 percent and 85 percent of their wages, respectively, as QREs based on retrospective interviews conducted by an outside consulting firm.

ACA's initial tax posture suffered from four acute legal defects directly implicated by Shami and related Fifth Circuit precedent. First, ACA kept no engineering timecards and relied entirely on the assumption that because ACA built tangible industrial prototypes, a federal court would be forced under United States v. McFerrin and Cohan to estimate a generous minimum wage allocation for Sterling and Vance. Second, while Sterling claimed he spent 75 percent of his year on the shop floor directing robotic welding trials, Chief Engineer Robert Miller and two shop-floor union foremen recently departed ACA on contentious terms and were prepared to testify that Sterling spent his time negotiating steel supply contracts, managing customer relations, and attending board meetings. Third, in violation of IRC § 41(d)(2)(C), ACA lumped all engineering, shop labor, and executive supervision into a single cost center, failing to separate research on the autoclave product from research on the robotic welding manufacturing process, and failing to track whether "substantially all" (80 percent) of the activities on each distinct business component constituted a process of experimentation. Fourth, ACA entered into a contract with a prime aerospace defense customer to develop the AeroCure-X prototype under a "capped cost-plus" reimbursement structure where ACA received progress payments regardless of whether the autoclave met final thermal uniformity tolerances, exposing the entire project to disqualification as "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).
Step 1: Bifurcating Business Components and Enforcing First-Line Engineering Governance

To comply with the statutory mandate of IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and the Fifth Circuit's strict supervisory rules in Shami, ACA must legally and operationally separate its R&D initiatives. Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii), any plant process, machinery, or technique for the commercial production of a business component must be treated as a separate business component from the product being produced, and the Four-Part Test must be satisfied independently for the process without taking into account research activities related to the product. Accordingly, ACA must configure its Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) and ERP accounting systems into two wholly independent project hierarchies: Business Component 1 (BC-Prod-01), covering the AeroCure-X Autoclave Pressure Vessel and Thermal Control System, and Business Component 2 (BC-Proc-02), covering the Automated Friction-Stir Robotic Welding Hull Assembly Line.

Furthermore, if the entire AeroCure-X autoclave vessel (BC-Prod-01) cannot satisfy the 80 percent Process of Experimentation test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) because 40 percent of the total labor involves routine structural steel fabrication and ASME code welding, ACA must invoke the "shrinking-back" rule of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2) at the outset of project tracking. Rather than claiming the entire vessel as a single business component and suffering total disallowance (as occurred in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), where the taxpayer's "all or nothing" strategy of claiming entire vessels left the court unable to apply the shrinking-back rule, and which cited Shami for the principle that the Cohan rule is not implicated unless the taxpayer first proves entitlement to some tax benefit), ACA must isolate the discrete sub-components where technical uncertainty actually resides: specifically Sub-Component BC-Prod-01A (Convective Gas-Vortex Manifold Sub-Assembly) and Sub-Component BC-Prod-01B (PID Multi-Zone Thermal Control Algorithm). Regarding executive wages, because Chief Engineer Robert Miller directly supervises the 22 engineers across these projects, Co-Chairman Sterling and VP Vance are second-tier executives whose managerial oversight is disqualified under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(2) and Shami. ACA must remove Vance completely from the claim and restrict any QRE allocation for Sterling exclusively to documented hours where Sterling personally participates in hands-on empirical testing sessions on the shop floor as a technical specialist.
Step 2: Eliminating Reliance on Cohan Estimation Through Contemporaneous Nexus Architecture

Because Shami held—applying the Fifth Circuit's rule that the earlier of two conflicting panel opinions controls—that Williams v. United States bars mandatory judicial estimation under Cohan when a taxpayer lacks a credible foundation proving that specific employees performed qualified services, ACA must eliminate any reliance on judicial approximation and build an audit-ready quantitative nexus. All 22 engineers, Chief Engineer Miller, and any participating shop technicians must log daily hours via biometric shop-floor terminals or PLM tickets tied directly to BC-Prod-01A, BC-Prod-01B, or BC-Proc-02, while logging routine structural fabrication to non-qualified production work orders.

To neutralize the exact risk of former-employee impeachment that undermined FSI in Shami (where former FSI employees James Sie and Ali Ghannad—the latter FSI's former Vice President of R&D—testified on the Commissioner's behalf), ACA must institute mandatory Contemporaneous Engineering Design Review and Test Logs. At the conclusion of every physical prototype weld trial or thermal chamber test run, the PLM system must generate an immutable PDF test log recording the date, duration, technical parameters tested, and every individual physically present and actively participating in the experiment. Crucially, the PLM workflow must require digital sign-off by Chief Engineer Miller and the shop-floor foreman before the engineering work order can be closed. If Co-Chairman Sterling actively participates in a four-hour pressure-cycle failure test, Miller's contemporaneous digital signature on that specific test log locks in the evidentiary record in real time, preventing Miller or union foremen from offering contradictory oral testimony years later in Tax Court.
Step 3: Structuring Experimentation Tracking to Satisfy the Substantially All Process of Experimentation Test

To prove that "substantially all" (80 percent or more) of the research activities on each designated business component constituted elements of a process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6), ACA must embed scientific method documentation directly into its Engineering Change Orders (ECOs) and simulation workflows. Every ECO and CAD/Finite Element Analysis (FEA) ticket opened under BC-Prod-01A, BC-Prod-01B, or BC-Proc-02 must require the lead engineer to populate four structured technical fields before labor hours can be billed:

headers: Concrete Technical Entry Required in ACA's PLM System

cells: 1. Objective Technical Uncertainty
IRC § 41(d)(1)(A); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3) (Capability, Method, or Design Uncertainty)

"Existing ASME pressure vessel designs and ACA engineering data cannot establish the manifold geometry required to maintain the specified thermal uniformity tolerance across a 12-meter composite load at 15 bar pressure without inducing turbulent boundary-layer separation."
2. Technical Alternatives Evaluated
IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5) (Evaluation of More Than One Alternative)
"Evaluating Alternative A (variable-pitch annular diffuser vanes with 14-degree blade angle) against Alternative B (dual-plenum counter-rotating impeller injection system)."
3. Systematic Experimental Process
IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) (Modeling, Simulation & Pilot Model Testing)
"Conducting 18 Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) turbulence simulations followed by physical thermocouple array testing on Pilot Model Hull Unit #1 across 10 pressurized thermal ramp cycles."
4. Granular Activity Hour Tagging
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) (Proving the ≥ 80% "Substantially All" Experimentation Fraction)

Tagging every engineering hour billed to BC-Prod-01A as either Qualified Experimentation (hypothesis formulation, CFD modeling, pilot testing, failure analysis) or Non-Qualified Support (routine BOM updates, standard code verification), ensuring that Qualified Experimentation hours ÷ total research hours ≥ 80%.

body.text: Step 4: Restructuring Customer Contracts to Defeat the Funded Research Exclusion

Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d), research is disqualified as "funded" to the extent it is funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. Courts determine whether research under a customer contract is funded by examining whether the taxpayer (a) retains "substantial rights" in the research results, and (b) bears the financial risk of failure—meaning payment is contingent upon the technical success of the research (as illustrated by the disallowance of capped cost-plus engineering contracts in Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States).

To prevent Project AeroCure-X from being disqualified as funded research, ACA must renegotiate its agreement with the aerospace prime contractor prior to commencing development, converting the arrangement from a capped cost-plus reimbursement contract into a Firm Fixed-Price, Performance-Contingent Contract. The amended contract must incorporate three explicit legal provisions: first, that all milestone payments and final contract consideration are strictly contingent upon ACA delivering a fully functional autoclave system that passes a formal Factory Acceptance Test (FAT) demonstrating the specified thermal uniformity tolerance at 15 bar across 10 consecutive thermal cycles; second, that if ACA's engineering design fails to achieve these strict technical tolerances, the customer holds the unconditional contractual right to reject the vessel, terminate the agreement for default, and receive a full refund of any prior milestone advances, placing the entire financial risk of research failure squarely on ACA; and third, that while the customer receives title to the single physical autoclave unit delivered, ACA retains exclusive ownership and unencumbered commercial rights to all underlying patents, CAD geometries, CFD models, PID control algorithms (BC-Prod-01B), and the automated friction-stir robotic welding manufacturing process (BC-Proc-02) for commercial deployment across all future customers without fee or restriction.
Synthesis of Remedial Governance and Compliance Architecture

The combined judicial holdings of the U.S. Tax Court and the Fifth Circuit in Shami v. Commissioner establish that while Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d) affords taxpayers reasonable flexibility in the form of their records, that flexibility never excuses the absence of an objective, verifiable nexus linking specific employees and hours to qualified first-line research activities. By contrasting the pre-remediation vulnerabilities against the post-remediation compliance architectures modeled in the two case studies, tax advisors and corporate legal counsel can systematically audit and fortify corporate R&D tax credit claims against IRS examination.

cells: Executive Wage Claims (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d))
Claiming 80% ("substantially all") of multi-million-dollar CEO/Co-Chairman salaries via retrospective oral estimates to capture 100% of compensation.

Abandoning the 80% cliff for executives; claiming exact fractional hours logged contemporaneously on bench/first-line technical tasks, benchmarked to reasonable technical compensation under IRC § 174(e).
Supervisory Hierarchy (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2))
Claiming wages of upper-level executives to whom the VP of R&D or Chief Engineer reports ("supervisor of the direct supervisor").
Restricting supervisory QREs strictly to first-line managers (VP of R&D / Chief Engineer) or establishing formal Tiger Team charters with direct bench reporting lines.
Technical Records & FRE 403 Probative Value
Proffering thousands of raw batch sheets or shop tickets with generic executive "Approved" stamps that fail to define the nature or duration of review.
Embedding structured Supervisory Action Logs inside ELN and PLM records capturing exact timestamps, technical uncertainties addressed, and specific scientific directives.
Testimonial Corroboration & Cohan Protection
Relying on self-serving executive testimony vulnerable to impeachment by former R&D staff, while hoping Cohan / McFerrin forces a court estimate.
Requiring contemporaneous multi-party digital sign-offs by subordinate engineers on all test logs and quarterly time summaries, eliminating reliance on Cohan estimation.
Business Component & Supply/Contract Segregation
Commingling product and process costs, relying on patent filings to prove wage QREs, and using informal POs or capped cost-plus customer contracts.
Bifurcating product vs. process components (IRC § 41(d)(2)(C)), isolating experimental supplies in dedicated GL accounts, and executing fixed-price, success-contingent contracts.

metaDescription: Shami v. Commissioner (5th Cir. 2014): uncorroborated time estimates and second-tier supervision cannot substantiate executive wage QREs.
